title: Australia’s chance to own the AI boom
full_text:
IN PARTNERSHIP WITH technology 1 Instead of merely importing the future, Australia can build it. TechnologyOne’s Ed Chung is calling on the nation to own its AI innovation – keeping intellectual property, value and sovereign potential at home The internet and cloud transformed the way Australians live and work. TechnologyOne chief executive Ed Chung says the artificial intelligence revolution sweeping global economies gives Brisbane – where the software company is based – the chance to do something differently: capture more of the value it creates.
For all the opportunity created by previous technology shifts, Chung sees a lesson in what Australia let slip away.
“With the internet and cloud, we were largely consumers of technology built elsewhere,” he says. “We adopted it, benefited from it, but much of the intellectual property, investment, jobs and tax revenue flowed offshore.” Artificial intelligence, he argues, presents an opportunity to change that equation.
“The biggest difference is that Australia doesn’t have to start from scratch,” Chung says. “AI presents a different opportunity because the value increasingly sits in industry expertise, trusted data and intellectual property. All these things can be developed right here.
“The opportunity isn’t simply to use more AI. It’s to own more of the value AI creates.” The argument has taken on greater urgency as governments grapple with how Australia should approach the rapidly evolving technology.
TechnologyOne, which first listed on the ASX in 1999, recently backed the Federal Government’s move to establish national AI standards and an Office of AI, while calling for governments to support Australian-developed technology through their own procurement decisions.
Chung believes Brisbane has many of the ingredients to capitalise on the sovereign AI that already exists locally: talent, universities, research capability and companies creating globally relevant technology.
“You need organisations prepared to take intellectual property to market,” he says. “You need customers willing to support local innovation. And you need a culture that believes world-class technology can be created from Brisbane, not just imported into it.” TechnologyOne is Chung’s case in point. Founded in Brisbane almost four decades ago, the company now invests more than $150m annually in research and development.
Its AI products Plus and Guide were conceived, designed and engineered in Brisbane, with the intellectual property owned locally and the technology governed under Australian laws and standards.
Plus is an agentic AI system that allows employees to interact conversationally with enterprise systems, while Guide helps students and residents navigate services. “For me, that’s what success looks like,” Chung says.
“Not simply using AI developed elsewhere but creating technology here that can compete anywhere in the world.” Brisbane will benefit from the AI revolution regardless, Chung argues. The question is whether it also captures the economic rewards of creating the technology, or remains a customer of companies based elsewhere.
For Chung, the question – who ultimately benefits from investment and growth? – also goes to the heart of the countdown to the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
“A genuine legacy isn’t a stadium,” he says. “It’s a young person finding a pathway into education. It’s a regional community gaining access to new opportunities. It’s a family experiencing better services, better outcomes or greater economic security.”
